questions.q: When does the @audited decorator function itself run for class PaymentService { @audited charge() {…} }?
questions.explain: The decorator runs once while the class is being defined and returns a replacement method. Only the wrapper it returns runs on every call. That is why setup work belongs in the decorator and the per-call work in the wrapper should stay small.
options: Every time charge is called
Every time a PaymentService is created
Once, when the class is defined
Only when the program is compiled

questions.q: A method decorator returns a new function. What happens to it?
questions.explain: For methods, getters and setters, a returned function replaces the original. Returning nothing keeps the original. The replacement usually calls the original with method.apply(this, args).
options: It is called once and its result is discarded
It replaces the original method on the class
It is added as a second method with the same name
It runs before the constructor

questions.q: Which plain JavaScript is closest to what @audited on the method charge does?
questions.explain: An instance method lives on the prototype. The decorator receives the original method and a context object, and its return value is written back in its place. The compiled code does exactly this inside a static block.
options: PaymentService.charge = audited
PaymentService.prototype.charge = audited(PaymentService.prototype.charge, context)
audited(new PaymentService())
class PaymentService extends audited {}

questions.q: Why does node account.ts (Node.js 24 type stripping) fail with SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token at @logged?
questions.explain: Decorators are a JavaScript feature, not a TypeScript type, so stripping leaves them in place. Until engines ship them, a compiler (tsc, esbuild via tsx, Babel with the decorators plugin) must rewrite them.
options: Because the decorator has a type annotation
Type stripping only removes types; @logged is JavaScript syntax that the engine does not support natively yet
Because experimentalDecorators is not enabled
Because decorators only work in CommonJS

questions.q: Why are the decorator examples in this lesson marked "Node.js only"?
questions.explain: The terminal's Babel setup rejects the syntax with "Support for the experimental syntax 'decorators' isn't currently enabled". On your computer, tsx or tsc compiles them. Applying a decorator by hand, as a function call, works everywhere.
options: Because decorators need the file system
Because browsers forbid classes in the terminal
The browser terminal compiles TypeScript with Babel, which is not configured for decorators, and browsers cannot run them natively
Because @ means something else in HTML

questions.q: What does a field decorator receive as its first argument?
questions.explain: Fields are created per instance, during construction. A field decorator can only return an initializer function that transforms each instance's initial value.
options: The field's current value
The class instance
undefined, because the field does not exist yet when the class is defined
A property descriptor

questions.q: You want to reject negative values every time stock is assigned. Why is a field decorator not enough?
questions.explain: accessor stock = 5 turns the field into a getter and setter pair over private storage, and an accessor decorator can wrap get, set and init.
options: Field decorators cannot throw
A field decorator only transforms the initial value; later assignments go straight to the field, so you need an accessor decorator that wraps set
Field decorators only work on strings
Because numbers are primitives

questions.q: A class has accessor stock = 5. Why is stock missing from Object.keys(product) and JSON.stringify(product)?
questions.explain: Auto-accessors store their value like #private fields. Code that serialises objects (API responses, logs) will not see them unless you add a toJSON method or map the object explicitly.
options: Because it is undefined
The value lives in a private slot, and stock is a getter and setter on the prototype, not an own property of the instance
Because accessors are static
Because the decorator deleted it

questions.q: In @retry(3), what is retry(3)?
questions.explain: Anything after @ is an expression that must evaluate to a decorator function. A factory lets the decorator take settings, captured in a closure.
options: The decorator itself, called with the method
A decorator factory call: it runs first and returns the actual decorator, which is then applied to the method
A type argument
A runtime check that the method was called three times

questions.q: @retry(3) is typed for methods that return a Promise. What happens when you put it on a synchronous balance(): number?
questions.explain: TypeScript checks a decorator as if it were called with the decorated value and its context (TS1241 for methods), and also checks that its return value can replace the original (TS1270).
options: It works but never retries
It throws when the class is defined
A compile error: decorators are type-checked like calls, and the method does not match the decorator's parameter type
TypeScript silently converts the method to async

questions.q: A method has @audit above @retry. When the method is called, whose wrapper runs first?
questions.explain: Decorators are applied from the closest outward, like function composition: audit(retry(method)). At call time the outermost wrapper runs first. So @audit @retry logs one audit entry per call, however many retries happen inside.
options: retry's, because it is closer to the method
audit's: retry is applied first and wraps the method, then audit wraps that result, so audit is the outermost layer
Both run at the same time
The order is not defined

questions.q: When is a class decorator applied, relative to the decorators on its members?
questions.explain: A class decorator receives the finished class, with its decorated members already in place, so it can register or wrap the class as a whole.
options: First, before any member decorator
Last, after all member decorators, when the class body is complete
In source order, mixed with members
Only when the first instance is created

questions.q: A method decorator calls context.addInitializer(fn) for an instance method. When does fn run?
questions.explain: Instance initializers run for every new object. Initializers added by static members and class decorators run once, right after the class is defined. That is why @bound can bind the method on each instance.
options: Once, when the class is defined
At the start of every constructor call, before field initializers, with this set to the new instance
The first time the method is called
Never, unless the class decorator calls it

questions.q: Why does const { total } = cart; total() work with @bound and fail without it?
questions.explain: In JavaScript, this depends on how a function is called, not where it was defined. Binding in an initializer gives every instance its own bound function, which also makes it safe to pass as a callback.
options: Because @bound makes the method static
A method taken off its object is called without this; @bound adds a copy bound to each instance, so this stays the cart
Because destructuring copies the class
Because @bound converts the method into an arrow function in the source

questions.q: Decorators wrote to context.metadata while defining Product. Where can other code read that object afterwards?
questions.explain: All decorators of one class share one metadata object, which is attached to the class under Symbol.metadata. Reflect.getMetadata is the unrelated legacy mechanism from the reflect-metadata library.
options: new Product().metadata
Product[Symbol.metadata]
Reflect.getMetadata("design:type", Product)
It is discarded after the class is defined

questions.q: Why does the lesson polyfill Symbol.metadata with Symbol.for("Symbol.metadata") rather than Symbol("Symbol.metadata")?
questions.explain: A symbol from Symbol() is unique, so esbuild-compiled classes would store metadata under a different key than your code reads. Symbol.for returns the same symbol for the same name everywhere in the process.
options: Symbol() cannot be assigned to Symbol.metadata
esbuild (and so tsx) falls back to Symbol.for("Symbol.metadata") when the real one is missing, so using the same registered symbol makes code compiled by either tool agree
Symbol.for is faster
Only Symbol.for symbols can be class keys

questions.q: A @column decorator does (context.metadata.columns ??= {})[name] = type. A subclass adds one column. Why does the parent class now list it too?
questions.explain: Metadata objects form a prototype chain like the classes do. Before writing, check Object.hasOwn(metadata, "columns") and, if missing, start from a copy of the inherited value.
options: Because the subclass decorator runs twice
The subclass's metadata object inherits from the parent's, so columns is found on the parent and ??= does not create a new one; the write goes into the parent's object
Because Symbol.metadata is shared by all classes
Because field decorators are static

questions.q: What does adding "ESNext.Decorators" to lib in tsconfig.json do?
questions.explain: lib describes what the runtime provides; it never adds anything. Declaring Symbol.metadata without providing it is a promise only a polyfill keeps.
options: It makes Node.js support decorators natively
It switches on experimentalDecorators
It declares Symbol.metadata and makes context.metadata non-optional in the types; the runtime still needs the polyfill
It adds the __esDecorate helpers to your bundle

questions.q: In the JavaScript tsc emits for a decorated class, where is the decorator actually called?
questions.explain: The static block runs once at definition time. __esDecorate builds the context object, calls the decorators closest-first, and writes the result onto the prototype with Object.defineProperty.
options: In the constructor, for every instance
In a static { … } block of the class, through the __esDecorate helper, while the class is being defined
In a separate file that tsc generates
Nowhere; tsc removes decorators

questions.q: A decorator is declared as function logged(target: object, propertyKey: string, descriptor: PropertyDescriptor). Which kind is it?
questions.explain: Legacy method decorators receive the prototype, the key and the property descriptor. Standard ones receive the method and a context object. The same @ syntax hides two incompatible calling conventions.
options: A standard method decorator
A legacy (experimentalDecorators) method decorator; in a standard-decorator project it fails with TS1241
A parameter decorator
A class decorator

questions.q: Can you write constructor(@Inject("clock") clock: Clock) with standard decorators?
questions.explain: Parameter decorators were left out of the standard (a separate proposal covers them). Standard-decorator frameworks pass dependency tokens explicitly, for example in a class decorator's arguments.
options: Yes, parameter decorators are part of the standard
No: parameter decorators exist only in experimentalDecorators; with standard decorators TypeScript reports "Decorators are not valid here"
Yes, but only for constructors
Only with emitDecoratorMetadata

questions.q: With emitDecoratorMetadata, a constructor parameter typed as the interface Clock is emitted as Object. Why?
questions.explain: Only classes survive compilation as values. That is why legacy DI frameworks still need @Inject(TOKEN) for interfaces, and why type-based autowiring is less automatic than it looks.
options: Because of a bug in tsc
Interfaces are erased and have no runtime value, so the only thing tsc can write is Object; a framework cannot tell which clock you wanted
Because Clock was not exported
Because metadata only stores primitives

questions.q: A NestJS-style project injects dependencies correctly after tsc, but in tests run through tsx (esbuild) every injected dependency is undefined. What is the likely cause?
questions.explain: Emitting parameter types needs the type checker, which esbuild does not have. The lesson's tsx example printed undefined for the same reason. Use a compiler that emits metadata for tests too, or explicit tokens.
options: The tests run in parallel
esbuild does not implement emitDecoratorMetadata, so the design:paramtypes metadata the framework reads is never written
esbuild does not support classes
tsx disables decorators

questions.q: Handlers register themselves with a class decorator. In production, order.refund has no handler, although refund-order.ts is decorated correctly. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: Registration by decorator happens when the module is evaluated. A module nobody imports (or one a bundler dropped as unused) registers nothing, and no compiler warns you. Import handler modules explicitly and check registrations at startup.
options: The decorator has a type error
No module imports refund-order.ts, so the class is never defined and its decorator never runs
Class decorators run lazily on first use
Two handlers were registered

questions.q: What does @CommandHandlerFor("order.place") from @zudojs/cqrs do on its own?
questions.explain: The decorator attaches the handler type to the class. A container or your startup code reads it and calls bus.register. It works with both decorator modes because it only uses the class it receives.
options: It registers the class on every command bus
It marks the class with metadata (readable with getCqrsType); your code still has to find the class and register it on a bus
It checks at compile time that execute accepts order.place
It only works with experimentalDecorators

questions.q: Which is the best use of a decorator?
questions.explain: Decorators suit cross-cutting rules that apply to many members and are not their business logic: auditing, retries, timing, permissions, registration. Logic that belongs to one method is clearer written inside it.
options: The pricing rules of one checkout method
An audit entry that every money-moving method must write
Parsing one API response
A calculation used in only one place

questions.explain: The field decorator's initializer transforms only the initial value, 3 into 6. The later assignment writes the field directly; the decorator never sees it.

questions.explain: The initial value goes through init, not set, and this decorator has no init, so -500 is stored unchecked. Later assignments are clamped. The accessor's value is private storage, so JSON.stringify shows nothing.
options:
0

email
email,rcNumber

questions.explain: The decorator runs once per class, so there is one calls variable for the method, shared by every instance. Per-instance state needs a WeakMap keyed by this, or an initializer.

questions.q: A decorator is applied by hand, twice by mistake. What does this print?
questions.explain: The second call wraps the already wrapped method, so one call passes through two wrappers. Stacking two identical decorators does the same. The @ syntax makes such duplication visible on the method.
options: [ 'topUp' ]
[ 'topUp', 'topUp' ]
TypeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded

questions.q: This wrapper calls the original method without passing this. What does it print?
questions.explain: method(...args) calls the original as a plain function, so this is undefined inside it. A wrapper must forward this: method.apply(this, args), and type it with a this parameter.
options:
calling count
1

calling count
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items')

calling count

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The marker is a static property on the class, and a subclass constructor inherits static properties from its parent. Code that discovers handlers by scanning classes would find two handlers for order.place, so discovery code should only register the classes it intends to.
options: order.place undefined
order.place order.place
undefined undefined
order.place PlaceBulkOrderHandler

questions.q: Write the method decorator logged: its wrapper calls the original with the same this and arguments, then logs NAME(ARGS) -> RESULT, and returns the result. It is applied by hand, so this runs in the browser terminal. The program should print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: The decorator reads the name once, at decoration time; the wrapper runs per call. method.apply(this, args) keeps this pointing at the wallet. With @logged on the method, the compiler would make exactly this replacement.

questions.q: Finish the retry(attempts) decorator factory for async methods: call the method; if it rejects and attempts remain, log NAME: retrying after "MESSAGE" and try again; after the last attempt, rethrow. The program should print the six lines shown.
questions.explain: retry(3) returns the decorator; the attempt count lives in its closure. return await inside try matters: without await, a rejection would escape the catch. Only retry operations that are safe to repeat, such as verifying a payment.
questions.expected:
verify: retrying after "timeout"
verify: retrying after "timeout"
PSK_7 verified
verify: retrying after "timeout"
verify: retrying after "timeout"
failed: timeout

questions.q: Write the field decorator trimmed: it returns an initializer that trims the initial value and collapses runs of whitespace to one space. The test calls the initializer directly. The program should print the two lines shown.
questions.explain: A field decorator receives undefined and returns an initializer, which runs for each instance's initial value. Testing it means calling that initializer; on a class, @trimmed address = " 12 Allen Avenue " would store the cleaned value.

questions.q: Write the accessor decorator nonNegative: return init and set that throw RangeError("NAME cannot be negative (got N)") for a negative value; set stores valid values through target.set. The test uses a hand-made target. The program should print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: Checking before calling target.set means a refused value never reaches the storage, so the old value stays. init covers the initial value, which set never sees.

questions.q: Fix column so that a subclass's metadata gets its own columns object, starting from a copy of the inherited one, before it writes. The test builds the metadata objects by hand, the way the runtime chains them. The program should print sku,priceKobo and then sku,priceKobo,shelfLifeDays.
questions.explain: Object.create(productMeta) is how a subclass's metadata inherits from its parent's. Object.hasOwn tells an inherited columns from an own one; copying it first keeps the parent's list unchanged.

questions.q: Write the class decorator factory handles(type): it stores the class in handlers under type, throws Error("two handlers for TYPE") if one is already there, and logs CLASSNAME handles TYPE. It is applied by hand. The program should print the four lines shown.
questions.explain: With @handles("order.place") on a class, this call happens when the class is defined, that is, when its module is imported. Refusing duplicates at registration turns a silent override into a startup error.
questions.expected:
PlaceOrder handles order.place
CancelOrder handles order.cancel
ORD-1 cancelled
Error: two handlers for order.place

questions.q: Write memoize for one-argument methods: cache results per instance (a WeakMap from instance to a Map) and per argument. It is applied by hand. The program should print 75000 75000 15000 and computed 2 times.
questions.explain: The WeakMap lives in the decorator's closure, once per method, but it is keyed by instance, so each object has its own cache and dropped objects can be garbage-collected. A plain Map keyed by argument alone would share results between instances.
